{{short description|Theorem that deals with the decompositions of complete hypergraphs}}
[[File:Complete-edge-coloring.svg|thumb|A partition of a [[complete graph]] on 8 vertices into 7 colors ([[perfect matching]]s), the case ''r''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2 of Baranyai's theorem]]
In [[combinatorics|combinatorial]] mathematics, '''Baranyai's theorem''' (proved by and named after [[Zsolt Baranyai]]) deals with the [[Glossary of graph theory#Independence|decompositions]] of complete [[hypergraph]]s.

==Statement of the theorem==
The statement of the result is that if <math>2\le r<k</math>  are integers and ''r'' divides ''k'', then the complete [[hypergraph]] <math>K^k_r</math> decomposes into [[graph factorization|1-factors]]. <math>K^k_r</math> is a hypergraph with ''k'' vertices, in which every subset of ''r'' vertices forms a hyperedge; a 1-factor of this hypergraph is a set of hyperedges that touches each vertex exactly once, or equivalently a [[Partition of a set|partition]] of the vertices into subsets of size&nbsp;''r''. Thus, the theorem states that the ''k'' vertices of the hypergraph may be partitioned into subsets of ''r'' vertices in <math>\binom{k}{r}\frac{r}{k} = \binom{k-1}{r-1}</math> different ways, in such a way that each ''r''-element subset appears in exactly one of the partitions.
==The case {{math|''r'' {{=}} 2}}==
In the special case <math>r = 2</math>, we have a complete graph <math>K_n</math> on <math>n</math> vertices, and we wish to color the edges with <math>\binom{n}{2}\frac{2}{n} = n-1 </math> colors so that the edges of each color form a perfect matching. Baranyai's theorem says that we can do this whenever <math>n</math> is even.

==History==
The ''r''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2 case can be rephrased as stating that every [[complete graph]] with an even number of vertices has an [[edge coloring]] whose number of colors equals its [[degree (graph theory)|degree]], or equivalently that its edges may be partitioned into [[perfect matching]]s. It may be used to schedule [[round-robin tournament]]s, and its solution was already known in the 19th century.  The case that ''k''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2''r'' is also easy.

The ''r''&nbsp;=&nbsp;3 case was established by R. Peltesohn in 1936. The general case was proved by [[Zsolt Baranyai]] in 1975.
